[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing intermittent fasting with high protein intake plus resistance training versus intermittent fasting with high protein intake alone, measuring resting energy expenditure via indirect calorimetry and fat-free mass via DXA at baseline, 8 weeks, and 16 weeks. — Directly tests the hypothesis by isolating the effect of adding resistance training to high-protein intermittent fasting on REE and fat-free mass preservation.

[PATH:empirical] Mechanistic study examining muscle protein synthesis and mechanotransduction signaling (e.g., mTORC1, YAP/TAZ activation) in response to resistance training during intermittent fasting with high protein intake, using muscle biopsies and phosphoprotein analysis. — Confirms the proposed mechanism (mechanotransduction signaling) that is claimed to mediate the attenuation of REE reduction.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of existing trials on intermittent fasting, protein intake, and resistance exercise, focusing on changes in REE and fat-free mass, with subgroup analysis by intervention type. — Aggregates available evidence to assess whether the combined intervention consistently shows a greater preservation of REE compared to high-protein fasting alone, and identifies gaps or confounding factors.

scope.domain: metabolic adaptation during caloric restriction with exercise intervention

qualifier.temporal: during active weight loss interventions lasting 8–16 weeks
qualifier.geographic: studied in healthy adults aged 18–50 in North America and Europe

[PATH:empirical] Controlled clinical trial comparing REE changes in participants on intermittent fasting with high protein intake vs. standard protein intake over 8 weeks, using doubly labeled water or indirect calorimetry. — Direct measurement of resting energy expenditure under controlled protein and fasting conditions would provide causal evidence to confirm or refute the hypothesis, addressing the disputed claim about REE impact.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing randomized controlled trials on intermittent fasting, high protein diets, and changes in fat-free mass and REE during caloric restriction of 4–12 weeks. — Synthesizing current evidence can clarify whether the preservation of fat-free mass from high protein intake consistently fails to prevent REE reduction, or if the hypothesis is supported by aggregated data.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of metabolic adaptation incorporating protein turnover costs and energy efficiency of intermittent fasting, based on existing physiological data. — A mechanistic model could predict whether high protein intake preserving fat-free mass should offset REE decline, helping to identify gaps in empirical evidence and guide future experiments.

[PATH:empirical] Controlled metabolic chamber study comparing 24h energy expenditure and NEAT (via accelerometry and indirect calorimetry) between high-protein intermittent fasting and high-protein regular feeding, with fasting windows ≥16h — Directly measures NEAT and REE under controlled conditions, isolating the effect of fasting intervals from protein-induced thermogenesis, which is key to confirming or refuting the hypothesized mechanism.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials examining the effect of intermittent fasting (with protein intake ≥25% of energy) on free-living physical activity energy expenditure (PAEE) and resting metabolic rate — Aggregates existing evidence to assess whether NEAT reductions are consistently observed across studies, and whether they occur independently of the thermic effect of feeding, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:theoretical] Mathematical model of energy partitioning during prolonged fasting, incorporating behavioral compensation (e.g., reduced spontaneous activity) and metabolic downregulation, parameterized with high-protein diet data — Provides a mechanistic framework to predict the magnitude of NEAT decrease required to explain observed REE reductions, and can be tested against empirical data to validate or refute the hypothesis.

qualifier.mechanism: compensatory behavioral and metabolic downregulation during prolonged fasting intervals

[PATH:empirical] Controlled crossover trial comparing 8 weeks of time-restricted feeding (16:8) with high protein (≥1.6 g/kg/day) vs. standard protein intake, measuring resting energy expenditure via indirect calorimetry and muscle protein synthesis via deuterium oxide or stable isotope tracer methods. — Directly tests whether high protein intake during intermittent fasting increases REE above fasting alone, with precise measurement of metabolic rate and protein synthesis.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials on intermittent fasting combined with protein supplementation, focusing on changes in resting metabolic rate, lean body mass, and markers of mitochondrial efficiency (e.g., PGC-1α, ATP production). — Synthesizes existing data to determine if the hypothesized effect is consistently observed across studies and populations, clarifying effect size and statistical significance.

[PATH:theoretical] Mechanistic study in human muscle biopsies or cell models examining how intermittent fasting and high protein intake modulate mTORC1 signaling, myofibrillar protein synthesis rates, and uncoupling proteins (e.g., UCP3) that may influence thermogenesis and energy expenditure. — Provides causal evidence for the proposed pathway: if high protein during fasting windows activates mTORC1 and increases muscle protein synthesis, and this upregulates uncoupling or futile cycling, it would support the metabolic rate enhancement mechanism.

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing intermittent fasting (e.g., time-restricted feeding or alternate-day fasting) with high-protein, unevenly distributed meals versus isocaloric continuous feeding with evenly distributed protein, measuring resting metabolic rate via indirect calorimetry and organ-specific mass changes via MRI or DXA at baseline, 12, 24, and 36 weeks. — Directly tests the causal claim under controlled conditions over the specified temporal and geographic scope, allowing measurement of RMR and differential organ mass loss.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal animal model study (e.g., rats or mice) on intermittent fasting with high-protein, skewed protein distribution, measuring liver, kidney, and skeletal muscle mass via dissection and histology, paired with whole-body calorimetry. — Provides mechanistic evidence for disproportionate organ mass loss and metabolic rate changes in a controlled setting, circumventing human ethical and compliance issues, and can inform human study design.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of existing literature on intermittent fasting, protein distribution, and resting metabolic rate changes, focusing on studies with ≥12-week follow-up and reporting organ-specific or lean mass compartment changes. — Synthesizes available evidence to assess consistency, effect size, and potential moderators, while identifying gaps and methodological limitations in prior work.
